node.label: Sidney Mintz
node.date_label: Worker in the Cane1960 · Sweetness and Power1985 · Three Ancient Colonies2010
node.description: Sidney Mintz joined Caribbean fieldwork to histories of labour, slavery, markets and consumption. Worker in the Cane presents the narrated life of Eustaquio “Taso” Zayas; Sweetness and Power traces sugar through colonial production and changing diets. With Richard Price he investigated Afro-American cultural formation. Three Ancient Colonies compares Jamaica, Haiti and Puerto Rico. His anthropological training and fieldwork shaped historical inquiries that connect workers’ experiences, Caribbean societies and wider economic change.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Worker in the Cane: A Puerto Rican Life History (1960); Caribbean Transformations (1974); With Richard Price, An Anthropological Approach to the Afro-American Past: A Caribbean Perspective (1976); Sweetness and Power: The Place of Sugar in Modern History (1985); Sweetness and Power — Penguin edition (1986); With Richard Price, The Birth of African-American Culture: An Anthropological Perspective — reissue with new preface (1992); Tasting Food, Tasting Freedom: Excursions into Eating, Culture, and the Past (1996); Three Ancient Colonies: Caribbean Themes and Variations (2010).
node.scope_note: Read Mintz’s three short author essays, selected2013 interview answers published2014, Leslie Rice’s1996 report, and Michiel Baud’s2011 review; complete monographs and the Mintz/Price primary essay and1992 preface remain unread. Baud’s reading of Caribbean Transformations is explicitly mediated, and he cautions that Three Ancient Colonies’s older fieldwork vignettes leave later migration, tourism and other changes insufficiently addressed. Original works, collections and reissues are distinct. Existing IDs, roster prose and source qualifications remain; no complete career interval or universal reception is inferred. proposed_edges.relationship: Sugar’s changing uses connect consumption to colonial production and industrial work
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Mintz’s “Sugar,” opening paragraphs1–8, explains the historical route from Caribbean fieldwork through a commodity’s global markets and human costs. His primary retrospective supports this scoped contribution; complete Sweetness and Power remains unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: A cane worker’s narrated life becomes a perspective on Puerto Rican labour history
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In the Thomas interview, sectionIV, Mintz explains returning to work with Taso and constructing a personal account alongside Puerto Rican history. The worker’s interpretation is part of the inquiry. Mintz’s claim to absolute disciplinary priority is not adopted.

proposed_edges.relationship: With Richard Price, cultural formation is studied through new circumstances and social institutions
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Baud(2011),263, explicitly identifies this joint1976/1992 inquiry. This named reader supports the scoped connection; it does not imply identical Afro-American cultures or prove influence on all Atlantic historians. Joint authorship and distinct editions are retained; primary essay unread.

proposed_edges.relationship: Plantation provisioning and peasant activity expose tensions within colonial economic organization
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Baud(2011),260, reads Caribbean Transformations as explaining provision grounds and emerging peasant practices within plantation society. This is Baud’s specific account of Mintz’s contribution, not a catalogue-derived argument or a general claim that all customary markets shared one logic.
